description: Hi, we are four students from TU Munich studying Applied & Engineering Physics, Astrophysics, Biomedical Engineering and Biology.
summary:
Mochi is an AI-powered astronaut wellbeing companion designed to make long-duration space missions more human. Instead of relying solely on dashboards and clinical-style alerts, Mochi lives on the astronaut's desktop as a friendly virtual pet that encourages healthy routines, supports private journalling, remembers conversations with consent, and gently nudges astronauts towards positive activities.
At its core is Dr G Zero, our Space Crew Neural Dynamics (SCND) intelligence engine, which analyses physical, behavioural and psychological indicators to identify emerging wellbeing patterns and potential risks. Fable 5.1 connects individual companions, enabling privacy-conscious coordination of crew activities and encouraging social interaction when it may be beneficial.

Mochi combines local AI through Ollama, personalised recommendations, adaptive gamification, mission challenges and a visual wellbeing dashboard. It aims to transform wellbeing monitoring from something astronauts are told to do into something they naturally engage with.

Our goal is to make space missions healthier, more connected and more human, because astronaut wellbeing is not just about surviving in space, but thriving together.
details:
Mochi — A Little More Than a Pet

What it does

Mochi is a little companion that lives on an astronaut's desktop. It gets to know them, plays with them, helps them reflect, and quietly brings the crew together. Mochi is not another health dashboard: it's a friendly character floating above the astronaut's other windows, with an explainable wellbeing intelligence one click behind it.

The project has three layers. In short: Dr G Zero thinks, Fable connects, and Mochi brings it to life.

•⁠ ⁠Mochi (the companion): click it to chat. It replies in short, natural messages using a small language model (Qwen3 4B through Ollama) that runs entirely on the astronaut's own computer. It offers a private journal, remembers only what the astronaut confirms, plays quick memory and reaction games, and suggests gentle activities. On request ("Mochi, show me my health") it opens the dashboard. Design for Mochi was hand-drawn, not AI-generated.

•⁠ ⁠Dr G Zero (the intelligence): monitors physical wellbeing (resting heart rate, heart-rate variability, blood oxygen, sleep, activity) and mental wellbeing through voluntary check-ins (mood, stress, fatigue, sleep quality, social connection, cognition). Its SCND engine (Sustained Change, Not Diagnosis) compares each astronaut only with their own baseline. A change counts only when three statistical detectors (persistence, EWMA and CUSUM) agree and it is confirmed over three days. The result is always one of YES, NO or INSUFFICIENT DATA, with every step explained. It links findings to an offline, cited registry of NASA Human Research Program risks.

•⁠ ⁠Fable (connection): lets each astronaut's companion coordinate activities people have agreed to, such as a game night, a shared meal or group exercise. It shares activity intents only, never journals, health data or emotional state. Today's build includes voluntary crew statuses, activity invitations and shared crew puzzles; the full Fable layer is planned.

•⁠ ⁠Gamification: healthy routines become play. Check-ins, prescribed exercise, rest and time with the crew move astronauts across the Solar System, build their habitat and unlock things for their pet. Rest is never punished, health metrics are never scores, and nothing is ever taken away.

Benefits and intended impact

On long missions, isolation, confinement and workload can wear down wellbeing gradually. Clinical tools tend to feel like surveillance, so people disengage from them. Mochi makes self-monitoring feel human and voluntary: astronauts engage because they want to. The value is in catching sustained change early and explainably, and pointing the astronaut toward human support while they stay in control. A YES suggests a private conversation with crew support, and the astronaut decides whether to share. The same approach could help anyone working in isolated or high-pressure settings, such as Antarctic stations, submarines or remote workers.

Tools and technology

•⁠ ⁠TypeScript, Electron, React, Node.js and SQLite, with zod validation and vitest.

•⁠ ⁠Ollama with Qwen3 4B for local AI. Measured on an Apple M1, the first words of a reply arrive in about 0.3 seconds (median).

•⁠ ⁠electron-builder for macOS and Windows installers; GitHub Actions for automated tests and builds; GitHub Pages for the website.

•⁠ ⁠Statistical methods: personal baselines with robust spread, EWMA, CUSUM, Mann–Kendall trend analysis, and an Isolation Forest that adds advisory insight but can never change a decision.

•⁠ ⁠Runs on an ordinary laptop. No special hardware, no cloud, no account.

How it's creative

Instead of adding another dashboard to an astronaut's day, we turned health monitoring into a relationship with a character. The intelligence is deliberately split from the personality: deterministic, auditable code makes every wellbeing decision, while the language model only puts it into kind words and can never change it. Fable reimagines crew wellbeing as companions helping friends get together, not managers watching people. Mochi itself is original hand-drawn artwork by our team.

Factors we considered

•⁠ ⁠Privacy: everything runs and is stored locally. Journals and health data never enter the language model's context, and nothing leaves the computer by default.

•⁠ ⁠Safety and ethics: Mochi never diagnoses depression or any other condition. A safety check runs before any AI involvement, and requests for help always get a fixed, serious response pointing to human support.

•⁠ ⁠Explainability: every result shows its data, method, baseline and uncertainty. With too little reliable data, Dr G Zero says INSUFFICIENT DATA rather than guessing.

•⁠ ⁠Autonomy and dignity: participation is voluntary, "personal space" is respected, and there are no rankings, competitive health metrics or hidden emotional monitoring.

•⁠ ⁠Honesty: all astronaut data in the demonstration is synthetic (five fictional crew members), thresholds are engineering defaults rather than clinical standards, and Mochi is not a medical device.

•⁠ ⁠Accessibility: works offline, with light and dark themes and keyboard-friendly games, and stays usable in a clearly labelled simple mode when no AI model is installed.
